MATH.G5.NUMBER.DIVISION.COMBINED_OPS_PRO.reveals: Ask the child to match stories to expressions, and include expressions with the operations in the wrong order.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DIVISION.COMBINED_OPS_PRO.help: Have the child act out the story step by step with counters, writing each step as it happens before combining them into one expression.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.error: Adds the same number to the numerator and denominator instead of multiplying both by the same number.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.cause: Believes 'doing the same thing to top and bottom' keeps a fraction the same, whatever the operation.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.reveals: Include the additive answer as a distractor in missing-number items; ask the child to shade 2/3 and 5/6 on fraction strips to check.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.help: Use a fraction board to show that 2/3 covers the same length as 4/6 but not 5/6, then link this to cutting each third into 2 pieces (multiplying by 2).

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.error: Changes only the denominator and leaves the numerator unchanged.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.cause: Sees the denominator as the only part that is 'converted' and does not see the fraction as a relationship between two numbers.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.reveals: Offer 3/8 as a distractor; ask 'Is 3/8 of a cake the same amount as 3/4 of the cake?' with a diagram.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.help: Fold a paper strip into quarters, shade 3, then fold again into eighths and count the shaded eighths.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.error: Thinks a fraction with bigger numbers is a bigger amount, even when the fractions are equivalent.

example.question: Wanjiku ate 1/2 of a chapati. Otieno ate 4/8 of the same-size chapati. Who ate more?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.cause: Applies whole-number thinking to the numerator and denominator separately.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.reveals: A compare-and-explain item with equivalent fractions written in different terms, with 'the one with bigger numbers' as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.EQUIVALENT_FRAC.help: Have children cut real or paper chapatis into halves and eighths and lay the pieces on top of each other.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.error: Simplifies by subtracting the same number from the numerator and denominator.

example.question: Simplify 6/9

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.cause: Thinks 'making the numbers smaller' is the aim, rather than dividing by a common factor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.reveals: Include the subtracted form as a distractor; ask whether 3/6 and 6/9 shade the same amount.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.help: Always ask 'What number divides both exactly?' and check the answer against a fraction chart.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.error: Divides once by a common factor and stops before reaching the simplest form.

example.question: Simplify 12/18

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.cause: Thinks 'simplify' means 'make it a bit simpler' rather than 'until no common factor except 1 remains'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.reveals: Use fractions needing more than one step (or one division by a larger factor) and offer the partly simplified form as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.help: Teach a final check: 'Do the numerator and denominator still share a factor other than 1?'

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.error: Believes a simplified fraction is a smaller amount than the original.

example.question: Is 2/3 of a bag of rice more than, less than or the same as 8/12 of the bag?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.cause: Thinks the size of the numbers shows the size of the fraction.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.reveals: A compare item pairing a fraction with its simplest form.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SIMPLIFY_FRACTI.help: Show both fractions on a fraction board and stress that simplifying renames the amount without changing it.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.error: Thinks the fraction with the larger denominator is larger.

example.question: Which is more: 1/4 of a loaf or 1/8 of the same loaf?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.cause: Uses whole-number ordering (8 > 4) and misses that more parts means smaller parts.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.reveals: Unit-fraction and same-numerator comparisons (e.g. 3/5 versus 3/8) where the 'bigger denominator' choice is wrong.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.help: Share one loaf among 4 children and then among 8, and ask who gets the bigger piece.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.error: Compares fractions of different-sized wholes as if the wholes were the same.

example.question: Akinyi got 1/2 of a small mandazi. Baraka got 1/4 of a large cake. Akinyi says she got more because 1/2 > 1/4. Is she right?
example.correct_answer: Not necessarily; 1/2 > 1/4 only when both are parts of the same (or equal) whole

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.cause: Treats fractions as fixed amounts and forgets they are parts of a particular whole.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.reveals: A compare-and-explain item using two clearly different wholes.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_LIKE_FR.help: Show half of a small orange beside a quarter of a watermelon and ask which is more food.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.error: Judges two fractions to be equal because each is 'one part short' of a whole.

example.question: Compare 2/3 and 3/4 using <, > or =

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.cause: Looks at the difference between the numerator and denominator rather than at the size of the parts.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.reveals: Pairs such as 2/3 versus 3/4 or 5/6 versus 11/12, with '=' as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.help: Compare the strips on a fraction board: the missing quarter is smaller than the missing third, so 3/4 is more.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.error: Picks the fraction with the bigger numerator and denominator as the larger.

example.question: Compare 5/12 and 2/3

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.cause: Whole-number bias: bigger numbers are taken to mean a bigger amount.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.reveals: Pairs where the fraction with larger terms is actually smaller.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.COMPARE_UNLIKE_.help: Require renaming to a common denominator, or a 'more or less than 1/2?' check, before deciding.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.error: Orders unit fractions by the size of the denominator, as if they were whole numbers.

example.question: Arrange 1/3, 1/6, 1/2 in increasing order

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.cause: Applies whole-number ordering to the denominators.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.reveals: Sets of unit fractions or same-numerator fractions to put in increasing order.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.help: Place the fractions on a fraction board or number line from 0 to 1 before writing the order.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.error: Orders fractions with different denominators by looking only at the numerators.

example.question: Arrange 2/3, 3/4, 5/12 in increasing order

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.cause: Does not see that numerators can only be compared once the parts are the same size.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.reveals: Mixed-denominator sets where numerator order differs from value order.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.help: Teach 'make the parts the same size first': rename to twelfths, order, then write back the original fractions.

example.question: Arrange 3/4, 1/4, 2/4 in decreasing order

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.cause: Has not linked the words 'increasing' and 'decreasing' to 'smallest first' and 'largest first'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.reveals: Paired items asking for both orders of the same set.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ORDER_FRACTIONS.help: Link the words to a picture, such as steps going up for 'increasing', and have children say 'smallest first' or 'largest first' before writing.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.error: Adds the denominators as well as the numerators.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.cause: Treats a fraction as two separate whole numbers and adds 'top with top, bottom with bottom'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.reveals: Offer the added-denominator answer as a distractor; ask whether 5/14 is more or less than 2/7 (it is less, which is impossible after adding).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.help: Use paper cut-outs: 2 sevenths and 3 sevenths make 5 sevenths, because the size of the pieces does not change.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.error: Adds the numerators and writes the answer as a whole number, dropping the denominator.

example.question: Mama used 2/8 of a packet of flour on Monday and 3/8 on Tuesday. What fraction did she use altogether?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.cause: Counts the pieces but loses track of what kind of pieces they are.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.reveals: Word problems where a whole-number answer is clearly unreasonable (5 packets).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_SAME_DENOMI.help: Have children say the unit aloud ('2 eighths plus 3 eighths is 5 eighths').

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.error: Subtracts the denominators as well as the numerators.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.cause: Treats the numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers to operate on.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.reveals: Include '2' or '2/0' as a distractor; use a number line marked in eighths.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.help: Model on a number line in eighths: start at 5/8, jump back 3 eighths, and land on 2/8.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.error: Cannot subtract a fraction from a whole, or gives the fraction taken away as the answer.

example.question: Juma had a whole pawpaw and ate 3/8 of it. What fraction is left?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.cause: Does not see that 1 whole can be written as 8/8.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.reveals: 'What is left?' word problems starting from a whole, with the subtracted fraction offered as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_SAME_D.help: Cut a real or paper pawpaw into 8 equal pieces, name the whole as 8/8, then remove 3 pieces.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.error: Adds the numerators and the denominators of unlike fractions without renaming.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.cause: Has no sense that only same-size parts can be counted together.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.reveals: Include 2/6 as a distractor; ask whether the answer can be less than 1/2 when 1/2 was one of the parts.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.help: Use a fraction board: put a half and a quarter end to end and find the single strip they match.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.error: Renames the denominator of one fraction but not its numerator, then adds.

example.question: Kamau bought 1/2 kg of sugar and then 1/4 kg more. How much sugar did he buy?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.cause: Sees renaming as 'making the bottoms match' rather than making an equivalent fraction.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.reveals: Ask for the renamed fraction as an intermediate step; the error shows as 1/2 = 1/4.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.help: Ask after every renaming: 'Is your new fraction the same amount as the old one?'

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.error: Renames a fraction by adding to the numerator and denominator instead of multiplying.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.cause: Carries over the additive idea of equivalence (see M_EQUIV_ADDITIVE).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.reveals: A 'spot the error' item showing a renaming step done by addition.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.ADD_ONE_RENAMIN.help: Go back to fraction strips to show that each third splits into two sixths, so 2/3 becomes 4/6.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.error: Subtracts the numerators and the denominators of unlike fractions without renaming.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.cause: Treats each fraction as two separate whole numbers.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.reveals: The wrong method gives an answer larger than the starting fraction; offer it as a distractor and ask whether that is possible.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.help: Get children to estimate first ('the answer must be less than 3/4') and check their result against the estimate.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.error: Renames only the denominator of one fraction, then subtracts.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.cause: Thinks renaming means changing the denominator so that the denominators match.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.reveals: Ask for the renamed fraction as a separate step.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.help: Get children to show the renamed fraction on a fraction chart before subtracting.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.error: Thinks the subtraction cannot be done (or reverses it) because the second fraction has bigger numbers.

example.question: Neema had 1/2 litre of milk and drank 3/8 litre. How much milk was left?
example.wrong_answer: It cannot be done because 3/8 is more than 1/2

MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.cause: Judges fraction size by the size of the numerators and denominators.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.reveals: Subtraction items where the second fraction has the larger terms but the smaller value.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.FRACTIONS.SUBTRACT_ONE_RE.help: Rename first, then compare: 1/2 is 4/8, which is more than 3/8.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.error: Gives whole-number place names to decimal places, for example calling the first place after the point 'tens', or thinks there is a 'oneths' place.

example.question: In 4.583, what is the place value of the digit 5?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.cause: Believes place value is symmetrical about the decimal point, or does not hear the '-ths' ending as meaning a part of one.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.reveals: Offer 'tens', 'tenths', 'ones' and 'hundreds' as options for the first digit after the point; choosing 'tens' or 'ones' exposes it.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.help: Use a place value chart with the ones column at the centre and stress the '-ths' ending, contrasting 10 shillings with one tenth of a shilling.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.error: Thinks a thousandth is larger than a tenth because a thousand is larger than ten.

example.question: Which is greater: 3 tenths or 3 thousandths?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.cause: Transfers the size of whole numbers to the names of fractional places, without seeing that more equal parts makes each part smaller.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.reveals: A 'which place is worth more?' item comparing tenths and thousandths, with no digits to distract.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_PLACE_NAME.M.help: Cut a strip or a chapati into 10 and then into 100 pieces so learners see that more pieces means smaller pieces.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..error: Gives the digit itself, or a whole-number value, as the value of a digit after the decimal point.

example.question: What is the value of the digit 8 in 4.583?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..cause: Has learnt place names as labels but does not connect them to quantities that are parts of one.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..reveals: Multiple choice with options 8, 80, 0.8 and 0.08 for the underlined digit.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..help: Ask learners to say the value aloud as '8 hundredths' and write it as both 8/100 and 0.08 before moving on.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..error: Leaves out zero placeholders when writing a decimal from words or a chart.

example.question: Write 'five and twenty-four thousandths' as a decimal.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..cause: Writes the digits heard ('twenty-four') straight after the point without checking that the last digit must be in the thousandths place.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..reveals: Dictate decimals whose words skip a place (e.g. 'three and seven hundredths') and check for 3.7 instead of 3.07.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_DIGIT_VALUE..help: Have learners write the words into a place value chart first, filling every empty column before the last named place with 0.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_LO.error: Thinks the decimal with more digits after the point is larger.

example.question: Which is greater: 0.5 or 0.125?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_LO.cause: Treats the digits after the point as a whole number (125 > 5).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_LO.reveals: Pairs where the shorter decimal is larger (0.5 vs 0.125, 0.8 vs 0.75); learners who always choose the longer one are exposed.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_LO.help: Have learners add zeros to make the same number of decimal places (0.500 vs 0.125) and compare tenths first on a chart.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_SH.error: Thinks the decimal with fewer digits after the point is larger because thousandths are 'tiny'.

example.question: Which is greater: 0.3 or 0.312?
example.wrong_answer: 0.3, because tenths are bigger than thousandths

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_SH.cause: Partial understanding that later places are smaller, applied to the whole number instead of to each digit.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_SH.reveals: Pairs where the longer decimal begins with the same digits and is larger (0.3 vs 0.312, 1.4 vs 1.45).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_SH.help: Show both on a number line from 0.3 to 0.4 so learners see 0.312 lies just beyond 0.3.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_TR.error: Thinks adding a zero at the end of a decimal makes it larger.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_TR.cause: Applies the whole-number rule that adding a zero on the right multiplies by ten.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_TR.reveals: Include '=' pairs such as 0.70 and 0.7, or 2.500 and 2.5, among comparison items.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_COMPARE.M_TR.help: Use money: 0.70 of a shilling and 0.7 of a shilling are both 70 cents.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_IGNO.error: Orders decimals by the digits after the point only, ignoring the whole-number part.

example.question: Arrange from smallest to largest: 2.05, 1.9, 1.875

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_IGNO.cause: Focuses on the decimal digits as the 'hard part', or reads them as whole numbers (5 < 9 < 875).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_IGNO.reveals: Sets where the whole-number parts differ and the decimal parts point the opposite way.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_IGNO.help: Teach a fixed routine: compare whole numbers first, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths, using a chart.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_WHOL.error: Puts a whole number first when ordering from smallest because it has fewer digits.

example.question: Arrange from smallest to largest: 3, 2.875, 2.95

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_WHOL.cause: Judges size by how many digits are written, not by place value.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_WHOL.reveals: Include a whole number in a set of decimals just below it.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ORDER.M_WHOL.help: Rewrite the whole number with zeros (3.000) and place all numbers on a number line from 2 to 3.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.error: Adds the whole parts and the decimal parts as separate whole numbers, without regrouping into the ones.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.cause: Sees the decimal point as a separator between two whole numbers, not as part of one place value system.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.reveals: Items where the tenths add to 10 or more, with 3.12 offered as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.help: Model with place value apparatus or coins that 12 tenths must be exchanged for 1 one and 2 tenths.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.error: Leaves out or misplaces the decimal point in the answer.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.cause: Treats the sum as a whole-number calculation and forgets that the point stays in line.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.reveals: Estimate-check items: 'Is the answer about 5 or about 5000?'
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_SAME_PLA.help: Ask learners to write the point in the answer row first, then estimate (4 + 1 is about 5) to check.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.error: Lines up the last digits on the right, as with whole numbers, instead of lining up the decimal points.

example.question: Wanjiru bought 3.5 kg of sukuma wiki and 1.25 kg of tomatoes. What is the total mass?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.cause: Over-applies the whole-number habit of right-aligning columns.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.reveals: Addends with different numbers of decimal places, set horizontally so the learner must arrange the columns.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.help: Have learners write 3.50 so both numbers have the same decimal places, and line up the points down the page.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.error: When adding a whole number to a decimal, places the whole number under the decimal digits.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.cause: Does not know that a whole number has an unwritten decimal point after its last digit.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.reveals: Whole number plus decimal items with distractors such as 0.31 or 0.85.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_ADD_MIXED_PL.help: Have learners rewrite whole numbers with a point and zeros (6 = 6.00) before adding.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.error: In each column, subtracts the smaller digit from the larger whichever number it belongs to, so no regrouping happens.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.cause: Believes you 'cannot take a bigger number from a smaller one', carried over from whole-number subtraction.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.reveals: Items needing regrouping in several columns; checking by adding (3.26 + 2.68 ≠ 5.42) exposes the error.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.help: Use place value apparatus to exchange 1 tenth for 10 hundredths, and always check by adding back.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.error: When regrouping across zeros, borrows straight from the ones but does not change the zeros in between.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.cause: Does not see that 6 ones must become 5 ones, 9 tenths, 9 hundredths and 10 thousandths.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.reveals: Items with zeros in the first number (6.003, 4.008) where regrouping must pass through them.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_SAME_PLA.help: Model exchanging one coin step by step down each column with apparatus before using the written method.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.error: When the second number has more decimal places, brings its extra digits straight down into the answer instead of subtracting them from zeros.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.cause: Treats empty places as 'nothing to do', not as zeros to subtract from.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.reveals: Items where the first number has fewer decimal places than the second.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.help: Have learners fill empty places with zeros (4.500) before subtracting, then check by adding.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.error: When subtracting a decimal from a whole number, subtracts only the whole parts and copies the decimal part.

example.question: Otieno had 7 litres of milk and sold 2.45 litres. How much is left?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.cause: Does not see that 7 = 7.00, so there are tenths and hundredths to take from.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.reveals: Change and 'how much is left' problems from a whole amount, with the copied-decimal distractor offered.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_SUB_MIXED_PL.help: Use a change context (Sh 7.00 minus Sh 2.45) and have learners write 7.00 first.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.error: Writes three zeros on the end of the decimal instead of moving the digits.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.cause: Over-applies the whole-number rule 'to multiply by 1000, add three zeros'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.reveals: Offer 2.45000 as a distractor and ask whether it is bigger than 2.45.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.help: Show on a place value chart that each digit moves three places to the left, and ask whether the answer should be bigger.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.error: Moves the digits the wrong number of places, often two.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.cause: Confuses multiplying by 100 with multiplying by 1000, or counts places loosely.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.reveals: Mix × 1000 items with answers from moving one, two and three places as options.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.help: Link to the three zeros in 1000 and have learners move one place per zero on the chart.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.error: Moves the point to the end of the digits and stops, without filling empty places with zeros.

example.question: A bag holds 3.2 kg of rice. How many grams is that? (3.2 × 1000)

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.cause: Thinks 'multiplying by 1000 removes the point' rather than shifting digits three places.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.reveals: Decimals with only one or two decimal places (3.2, 0.04) multiplied by 1000.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.help: Have learners count three jumps of the point, writing a 0 in each empty place.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.error: Moves the digits to the right, making the number smaller.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.cause: Learnt 'move the point three places' as a rule without a sense of whether the answer should grow.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.reveals: Ask learners to estimate first: should 4.6 × 1000 be more or less than 4.6?
MATH.G5.NUMBER.DECIMALS.DEC_MULT_1000.M_.help: Always start with an estimate, e.g. 4.6 kg is more than 4000 g, so the answer must be in the thousands.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.error: Reads '=' as 'now write the answer' and works left to right, ignoring what comes after the sign.

example.question: Fill in the box: 8 + 4 = □ + 5

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.cause: Years of sums of the form 'a + b = □' have taught that '=' signals the result of an operation, not equal value on both sides.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.reveals: Put the box or the operation on the right of '=', and include 12 and 17 as distractors.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.help: Use a balance scale or bundles of sticks and ask 'Is it the same on both sides?' Regularly write equations such as 12 = 7 + 5 with the operation on the right.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.error: Thinks a letter stands for an object or a word (p = pen) instead of a number such as the cost or the count.

example.question: A pen costs p shillings. What does p stand for?
example.correct_answer: the cost of one pen in shillings (a number)

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.cause: Letters are used as abbreviations elsewhere (kg, m, sh), so the child treats a letter as a label rather than as an unknown number.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.reveals: Ask what the letter stands for, with options 'a pen', 'pens' and 'the number of shillings one pen costs'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.help: Always define letters in full, e.g. 'Let p be the number of shillings one pen costs', and ask learners to say the definition aloud.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.error: Calls an expression such as x + 7 an equation, or does not see that an equation must contain '=' with two equal sides.

example.question: Which is an equation? A: x + 7   B: x + 7 = 15   C: 15

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.cause: The Grade 4 work on expressions and this Grade 5 work both use letters, so any letter-and-number string is seen as 'algebra' or 'an equation'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.reveals: A sorting task mixing expressions, equations and plain numbers.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_MEANI.help: Contrast pairs side by side: 'x + 7' (a description you cannot solve) and 'x + 7 = 15' (a balance you can solve).

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.error: Writes the subtraction in the order the numbers appear, not in the order of the action.

example.question: Njeri had some shillings. She spent sh 50 on mandazi and was left with sh 120. Let n be the number of shillings she had. Write an equation.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.cause: The child treats subtraction as commutative, or copies the numbers in story order without modelling 'start amount minus amount spent'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.reveals: A multiple-choice item with both orders offered, or asking the learner to test their equation with a sensible value.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.help: Act the story out with real coins: start with an unknown pile, take 50 away, and write the equation in the order the actions happened.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.error: Sees 'more' and adds the given numbers, or writes the opposite operation, instead of modelling the comparison.

example.question: Otieno has 15 eggs. That is 6 more than Akinyi has. Let a be the number of eggs Akinyi has. Write an equation.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.cause: Reliance on key words ('more' means add) rather than on the relationship between the two quantities.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.reveals: Comparison stories where the key word points to the wrong operation, with a − 6 = 15 and 15 + 6 = a as distractors.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.help: Draw a bar model with Akinyi's bar plus 6 matching Otieno's 15, and ask 'Who has more?' before writing anything.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.error: Works out the answer mentally and writes only 'p = 11' when asked to form the equation.

example.question: A matatu had some passengers. At Kisumu 7 more got in, making 18. Let p be the number of passengers at first. Form an equation.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.cause: The child sees the equation as an extra step with no purpose and jumps to the arithmetic, so they do not separate modelling from solving.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.reveals: Ask only for the equation, or use numbers large enough that mental shortcuts fail (e.g. p + 1,375 = 4,020).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.help: Mark forming and solving as separate steps, and explain that the equation is a record of the story that anyone can check.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.error: Puts the multiplier on the wrong quantity in a 'times as many' statement.

example.question: A farmer in Nakuru has 4 times as many goats as cows. He has 24 goats. Let c be the number of cows. Write an equation.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.cause: The child translates the words in order ('4 times … goats') instead of asking which group is bigger.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.reveals: Offer c = 4 × 24 as a distractor, and ask whether the farmer then has more cows than goats.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.help: Before writing, ask 'Which is more, cows or goats?' and check that the equation makes the larger group bigger.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.error: Writes the divisor first in an equal-sharing equation.

example.question: Mama bought x oranges and shared them equally among 5 children. Each child got 6. Write an equation.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.cause: The child believes division can be written in any order, as with multiplication.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.reveals: Multiple choice with both orders offered; or ask the learner to share 30 counters and see which equation fits.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.help: Model with counters: the total being shared always comes first, before the ÷ sign.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.error: Writes 3 + b instead of 3b (3 × b) for the cost of 3 identical items.

example.question: 3 exercise books each cost b shillings. Together they cost sh 45. Write an equation.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.cause: The child joins the numbers in the story with the most familiar operation and does not see the equal groups.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.reveals: A distractor 3 + b = 45; or ask the learner to substitute b = 15 into their equation and check against the story.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_FORM_.help: Write b + b + b = 45 first, then show that this is the same as 3b, linking back to simplifying expressions in Grade 4.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: Applies the operation that is in the equation instead of its inverse.

example.question: Solve x + 15 = 40

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: The child sees '+' and adds the two numbers, so they do not think of 'undoing'.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: The distractor 55; asking the learner to substitute shows 55 + 15 ≠ 40.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: Make checking by substitution a required last line, and use a balance picture: take 15 off both sides.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: For x − a = b, subtracts the smaller number from the larger instead of adding.

example.question: Solve x − 18 = 30

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: The child sees '−' and subtracts, or always takes the smaller number from the larger.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: The distractor 12; substituting gives 12 − 18, which cannot equal 30.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: Tell the story aloud ('I had some, gave away 18, have 30 left; did I start with more or less than 30?') before calculating.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: Solves a − x = b by adding, as if it were x − a = b.

example.question: Solve 50 − x = 20

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: The child overgeneralises a learned rule ('minus becomes plus') without noticing where the unknown sits.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: Mix a − x = b items in with x − a = b items, and include a + b as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: Read 50 − x = 20 as 'What must I take from 50 to leave 20?' and check by substitution.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: Multiplies the two numbers when solving ax = b.

example.question: Solve 4x = 28

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: The child sees multiplication in the equation and repeats it instead of undoing it.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: The distractor 112; asking whether 4 groups of 112 make 28.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: Read 4x = 28 as '4 groups of what make 28?', and connect it to the multiplication–division family 4 × 7 = 28, 28 ÷ 4 = 7.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: Reads 3x as a two-digit number 'thirty-something' and fills in a digit.

example.question: Solve 3x = 36

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: Place-value habits: in arithmetic, writing digits side by side means tens and ones, not multiplication.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: Items where the digit pattern gives a plausible but wrong answer (3x = 36, 2x = 24, 4x = 48).
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: Write 3 × x alongside 3x until learners say '3 times x' automatically, and check that 3 × 6 = 18, not 36.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: For x ÷ a = b, divides b by a (or subtracts) instead of multiplying.

example.question: Solve x ÷ 5 = 8

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: The child applies the operation they can see, or does not understand that the total being shared must be the biggest number.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: Remainder-type or subtraction-type distractors; substitution shows that 3 ÷ 5 is not 8.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: Use the sharing story ('shared among 5, each got 8, so how many were there altogether?') with counters.

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: Operates on the numbers in the order they appear, following a key word, without modelling the situation.

example.question: A matatu had some passengers. At Kisumu 6 got off and 9 remained. How many were in the matatu at first?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: The child reads 'got off' as 'subtract' and subtracts the smaller number from the larger, skipping the equation.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: Stories where the key word suggests the wrong operation, with that answer as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: Insist on writing the equation from the story first, then ask 'Should the starting number be more or less than 9?'

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.error: Accepts an answer that does not make sense in the story because they never check it against the context.

example.question: 5 bunches of sukuma wiki cost sh 150. How much does one bunch cost?

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.cause: The child sees solving as symbol-pushing, separate from the real situation, and does not interpret the result.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.reveals: Ask 'Is this answer reasonable? Why?', or offer sh 750 as a distractor.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_SOLVE.help: End every problem with a sentence answer and the question 'Does one bunch cost less than five bunches?'

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_TWO_S.error: Divides first and then subtracts, undoing the operations in the wrong order.

example.question: Solve 2x + 6 = 20

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_TWO_S.cause: The child divides only part of the left side, not seeing that both 2x and 6 make up the 20.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_TWO_S.help: Use a balance or parcel model: first remove the loose sh 6 from both sides, then share what is left into 2 equal parts.

example.question: Solve 2x + 6 = 20

MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_TWO_S.cause: The child wants a single-term answer and does not understand that letter terms and number terms are unlike.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_TWO_S.reveals: A worked solution showing 8x = 20 for learners to judge; or an open item where 8x appears in working.
MATH.G5.NUMBER.SIMPLE_EQUATIONS.EQ_TWO_S.help: Revisit Grade 4 simplifying with objects: 2 pens and 6 shillings cannot become 8 pens.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.error: The child picks a unit that does not suit the size of the distance, for example metres or centimetres for the distance between towns.

example.question: Which unit is best for measuring the distance from Nairobi to Nakuru: cm, m or km?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.cause: The child has not yet linked unit size to the size of the thing measured, and m is the largest unit used so far.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.reveals: A unit-choice item with cm, m and km options for a town-to-town distance; choosing m or cm exposes it.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.help: Ask how many metre sticks it would take to reach the next town, so learners feel why counting in metres is impractical.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.error: The child confuses km with kg because both start with 'kilo', and writes distances in kg or masses in km.

example.question: Write the distance shown on the road sign 'Thika 12': Thika is 12 ___ away.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.cause: The child remembers the 'kilo' prefix but not what quantity each unit measures.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.reveals: A unit-completion item that includes kg as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_IDENTIFY_UNIT.M.help: Pair each unit with what it measures ('km – how far', 'kg – how heavy') on a classroom chart, and sort real examples into the two groups.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.error: The child gives estimates far too large or too small because they have no sense of how long 1 km is.

example.question: Amina walks to school in about 15 minutes. About how far is her school: 1 km, 50 km or 10 m?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.cause: The child has no personal benchmark for a kilometre and chooses by the look of the number.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.reveals: A multiple-choice estimate with options differing by powers of ten.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.help: Walk or pace a measured 1 km (or 2½ laps of a 400 m track) with the class and time it, so learners have a felt benchmark.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.error: The child gives a time instead of a distance when asked how far a place is.

example.question: Estimate how far the market is from your school.
example.correct_answer: a distance in km, e.g. about 2 km

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.cause: In everyday talk people answer 'how far?' with a travel time, so the child does not separate the two.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.reveals: An open estimation item that requires a unit; answers in minutes or hours expose it.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_ESTIMATE_DISTAN.help: Accept the time as a clue, then ask 'how many km do you walk in that time?' to turn it into a distance.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..error: The child says 1 km = 100 m (or 10 m), carrying over the m–cm relationship from Grade 4.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..cause: The child overgeneralises '1 m = 100 cm' to every pair of units.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..reveals: A direct fill-in, or a 'how many 100 m make 1 km?' item where the answer 1 exposes it.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..help: Mark ten 100 m stretches on the school field or road and count them together to make 1 km.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..error: The child compares only the numbers and ignores the units, so thinks 1 500 m is longer than 2 km.

example.question: Which is longer: 2 km or 1 500 m?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..cause: The child focuses on the size of the numeral, not the size of the unit.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..reveals: Comparison items where the shorter distance has the larger numeral.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.KM_M_RELATIONSHIP..help: Require both distances to be written in the same unit before comparing.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.error: The child multiplies by 100 instead of 1 000 when changing km to m.

example.question: Convert 6 km to metres.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.cause: The child applies the Grade 4 m-to-cm factor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.reveals: A distractor of 600 m in a multiple-choice conversion.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.help: Have learners say '1 km is 1 000 m, so 6 km is 6 lots of 1 000 m' before writing the answer.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.error: The child writes the km and m digits side by side, leaving out the zeros needed in the hundreds or tens place.

example.question: Convert 3 km 45 m to metres.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.cause: The child joins the digits instead of adding 3 000 m + 45 m, and does not see the metres as needing three places.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.reveals: Mixed measures with fewer than 100 m (e.g. 2 km 5 m, 3 km 45 m); answers like 345 or 2 500 expose it.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_KM_TO_M.M_.help: Use a place-value chart with the km digit in the thousands column and the metres always filling three columns.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.error: The child divides by 100 (splits off two digits) instead of 1 000 when changing m to km.

example.question: Write 3 400 m in km and m.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.cause: The child applies the Grade 4 cm-to-m pattern.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.reveals: A distractor of 34 km, or 34 km 0 m, in a conversion item.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.help: Ask 'how many whole thousands of metres are there?' and circle the thousands digit as the km.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.error: The child splits the number in the wrong place, or drops a zero, when the metres part has an internal zero.

example.question: Write 4 050 m in km and m.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.cause: The child reads the leftover digits as a number without keeping their place value.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.reveals: Values like 4 050 m or 7 008 m, with distractors 4 km 5 m and 40 km 50 m.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.CONVERT_M_TO_KM.M_.help: Check by converting back: 4 km 5 m gives 4 005 m, which is not 4 050 m.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_NO_.error: The child leaves 1 000 m or more in the metres column instead of regrouping it as km.

example.question: 2 km 700 m + 1 km 600 m

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_NO_.cause: The child adds the columns separately and does not see that 1 000 m must become 1 km.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_NO_.reveals: Addition items where the metres total 1 000 or more; answers with a metres part of 1 000 or more expose it.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_NO_.help: Have learners check that the metres part is always less than 1 000 and regroup if it is not.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_REG.error: The child regroups when the metres reach 100, as they did with metres and centimetres in Grade 4.

example.question: 2 km 70 m + 1 km 50 m

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_REG.cause: The child applies the m–cm exchange rate (100) to km–m.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_REG.reveals: Items where the metres total between 100 and 999, so no regrouping should happen.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_REG.help: Write '1 000 m = 1 km' at the top of the column work and ask 'have we reached 1 000 m yet?'

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_IGN.error: The child adds a km value and a m value as plain numbers, ignoring the different units.

example.question: A matatu travels 5 km, then 300 m more. How far altogether?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_IGN.cause: The child does not check units before adding.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_IGN.reveals: An item mixing a pure km value with a pure m value.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.ADD_KM_M.M_ADD_IGN.help: Have learners write both measures under km and m column headings before adding.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.error: In the metres column the child takes the smaller number from the larger, whichever is on top, instead of exchanging 1 km.

example.question: 5 km 200 m − 2 km 650 m

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.cause: The child believes you always subtract the smaller digit or number from the larger.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.reveals: Items where the metres being taken away are more than the metres on top.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.help: Check by adding: 3 km 450 m + 2 km 650 m gives 6 km 100 m, not 5 km 200 m.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.error: When exchanging, the child turns 1 km into 100 m instead of 1 000 m.

example.question: 4 km 50 m − 1 km 80 m

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.cause: The child applies the Grade 4 exchange of 1 m = 100 cm.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.reveals: Items with small metre values needing an exchange, such as 50 m − 80 m.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.help: Have learners write the exchanged metres in full (1 000 + 50 = 1 050 m) above the column before subtracting.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.error: The child exchanges 1 km into the metres correctly but forgets to reduce the km by 1.

example.question: 5 km 200 m − 2 km 650 m

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.cause: The child sees the exchange as just 'adding 1 000' to the metres, not as moving 1 km across.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.reveals: Exchange items; an answer exactly 1 km too large exposes it.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.SUBTRACT_KM_M.M_SU.help: Have learners cross out the km digit and write the new value each time they exchange.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.error: The child leaves the product of the metres as 1 000 m or more instead of regrouping it into km.

example.question: A boda boda rider makes 3 trips of 2 km 400 m each. How far does he ride?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.cause: The child multiplies the columns separately without applying 1 000 m = 1 km.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.reveals: Items where the metres × multiplier is 1 000 or more.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.help: Have learners multiply the metres first and regroup before multiplying the km, as in column multiplication.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.error: The child multiplies only the km (or only the metres) and copies the other part unchanged.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.cause: The child treats the measure as a whole number with a label attached, not as two parts that both scale.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.reveals: Distractors with only one part multiplied.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.MULTIPLY_KM_M.M_MU.help: Show the multiplication as repeated addition of the whole measure (1 km 300 m four times) so learners see both parts grow.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.error: The child divides the km and m separately and drops the remainder from the km.

example.question: A road 7 km 200 m long is shared equally among 4 groups to clean. How much does each group clean?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.cause: The child sees the two parts as separate numbers and does not know the leftover 3 km must be carried into the metres.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.reveals: Items where the km do not divide exactly by the divisor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.help: Have learners check by multiplying: 1 km 50 m × 4 = 4 km 200 m, not 7 km 200 m.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.error: The child carries the remaining km into the metres as 100 m each instead of 1 000 m.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.cause: The child applies the Grade 4 m–cm factor when carrying the remainder (3 km taken as 300 m, so 500 m ÷ 4 = 125 m).
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.reveals: Items with a km remainder, with a distractor built on the 100 m error.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.LENGTH.DIVIDE_KM_M.M_DIV_.help: Offer the 'convert everything to metres first' method (7 200 m ÷ 4) as a check.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_C.error: Writes area in cm (a length unit) instead of cm².

example.question: A rectangle is 4 cm long and 3 cm wide. What is its area?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_C.cause: The child sees the unit as a label copied from the sides, not as a description of what was counted (squares).
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_C.reveals: Offer options 12 cm, 12 cm² and 14 cm. Alternatively, ask the child to write their own unit and say what it means.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_C.help: Every time an area is recorded, have the child point to one 1 cm by 1 cm square and say 'we counted twelve of these', then write cm².

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_S.error: Reads the small '2' in cm² as 'times 2' or '2 cm', so thinks 5 cm² means 10 cm.

example.question: What does 5 cm² mean?
example.correct_answer: The space covered by 5 squares, each 1 cm by 1 cm

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_S.cause: The child does not yet know index notation, so the superscript is taken as an ordinary number to use.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_S.reveals: Ask the child to draw 5 cm² on 1 cm grid paper. A child with this error draws a 10 cm line or 10 squares.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_S.help: Read cm² aloud as 'square centimetres' and always pair the symbol with a picture of square tiles until the meaning is secure.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_A.error: Thinks any single square, whatever its size, has an area of 1 cm².

example.question: A square has sides of 2 cm. What is its area?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_A.cause: The child links 'one square' with 'one square centimetre', ignoring the 1 cm side length.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_A.reveals: Show a 2 cm square drawn as a single outline, with no grid inside, and ask for its area in cm².
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_UNIT_MEANING.M_A.help: Have the child cover a 2 cm square with 1 cm cut-outs, so they see it takes four.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.error: Leaves gaps between cut-outs or lets them overlap or hang over the edge, then counts them.

example.question: Cover a postage stamp 3 cm by 2 cm with 1 cm squares. What is its area?
example.wrong_answer: 4 cm² (squares spaced out with gaps) or 8 cm² (overlapping)

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.cause: The child sees covering as 'putting squares on it' and does not understand that area means filling the space exactly.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.reveals: Show a picture of a covering with visible gaps and ask whether the count gives the area, and why.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.help: Have pupils check each other's coverings for gaps and overlaps before counting, and discuss why each one makes the count wrong.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.error: Counts grid lines or dots along the edges instead of the squares.

example.question: A rectangle on 1 cm grid paper is 5 squares long and 3 squares wide. Find its area.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.cause: The child focuses on the marks (lines or points) rather than the spaces between them.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.reveals: Include 24 cm² as an option, or ask the child to show which things they counted.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.help: Have the child shade or put a counter in each square as they count, so the spaces are counted, not the lines.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.error: Counts only the squares around the edge of the shape and misses the inside ones.

example.question: A rectangle on 1 cm grid paper is 4 squares long and 3 squares wide. Find its area.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.cause: The child confuses the boundary with the whole surface, an early form of mixing up area and perimeter.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.reveals: Use rectangles at least 3 by 4 so that inside squares exist, and include the border count as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_COVER_AND_COUNT.help: Have the child colour the border squares in one colour and the inside squares in another, then add both counts.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_REAL_LIFE.M_CM2_.error: Chooses cm² for things that are lengths, such as the length of a pencil or the height of a desk.

example.question: Which would you measure in cm²: the length of a pencil, the top of a postage stamp, or the mass of a mango?
example.correct_answer: The top of a postage stamp

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_REAL_LIFE.M_CM2_.cause: The child knows cm² has 'cm' in it, so links it with anything measured with a ruler.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_REAL_LIFE.M_CM2_.reveals: Use matching tasks that put a length quantity next to a surface, with both cm and cm² offered.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.CM2_REAL_LIFE.M_CM2_.help: Have the child run a finger along a length but rub a palm over a surface, and say 'cm for along, cm² for covering'.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.error: Adds the number of rows and the number of columns instead of multiplying them.

example.question: A tray of mandazi is laid out in 6 rows with 4 in each row, each taking up 1 cm² on a drawing. What is the area?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.cause: The child sees two numbers and adds by default, without seeing the array as repeated rows.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.reveals: Include the sum as a distractor, and ask the child to check by counting one row and skip-counting.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.help: Have the child skip-count the rows aloud (4, 8, 12, …, 24) and then record this as 6 × 4.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.error: When only the first row and first column of squares are drawn, counts just the drawn squares.

example.question: A rectangle shows 4 squares along the top and 3 squares down the side; the rest is blank. What is its area?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.cause: The child does not yet picture the rectangle as filled with equal rows, so counts only what is visible.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.reveals: Present partly drawn grids, which separate array thinking from plain counting.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_ROWS_BY_COLUMNS.help: Have the child finish drawing the rows with a ruler, then predict the area of the next partly drawn grid before drawing it.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.error: Adds the sides (finding the perimeter, or just length + width) instead of multiplying.

example.question: Find the area of a rectangle 7 cm long and 5 cm wide.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.cause: Perimeter was learnt with the same diagrams, and the child links 'work out' with adding the sides.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.reveals: Give options 12, 24 and 35 with mixed units, and set area and perimeter questions on the same figure.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.help: On the same rectangle, have the child trace the edge for perimeter and shade the inside for area, saying which they are finding before calculating.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.error: For a square, multiplies the side by 2 instead of by itself.

example.question: A square tile has sides of 6 cm. What is its area?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.cause: The child may read the '²' as ×2, or forget that a square has a length and a width that are equal.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.reveals: Use square questions with side × 2 as a distractor. Sides of 2 cm do not reveal the error, because 2 × 2 = 2 + 2.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.help: Label both the length and the width of the square (6 cm and 6 cm) before multiplying, and check by drawing the array.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.error: Multiplies all four labelled side lengths together.

example.question: A rectangle has its sides labelled 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm. Find its area.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.cause: The child remembers 'multiply the sides' without understanding that length × width counts rows of squares.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.reveals: Label all four sides on the diagram, and ask whether 225 squares could fit on a 5 by 3 grid.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_RECT_SQUARE_CAL.help: Have the child sketch the 5 by 3 array and check whether their answer is sensible against it.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_CONT.error: In a word problem that needs area, works out the perimeter (or the other way round).

example.question: Akinyi wants to cover the top of a box 20 cm long and 15 cm wide with kitenge cloth. How many square centimetres of cloth does she need?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_CONT.cause: The child picks out the numbers and an operation without picturing whether the context is about covering or going around.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_CONT.reveals: Set paired problems on the same box: one about ribbon around the edge and one about cloth covering the top.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_CONT.help: Have the child first say whether the task is 'covering' or 'going around' and sketch it before choosing the operation.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_MISS.error: To find a missing side from the area, subtracts the known side from the area instead of dividing, or writes the side in cm².

example.question: Otieno's exercise book cover has an area of 48 cm² and a length of 8 cm. What is its width?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_MISS.cause: The child does not see the missing side as the missing factor in length × width = area, and mixes up length units and area units.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_MISS.reveals: Include the area minus the side and a side written in cm² as distractors.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.AREA.AREA_PROBLEMS.M_MISS.help: Write '8 × ? = 48' and find the missing number on a multiplication chart, then say 'a side is a length, so cm'.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..error: The child writes volume in cm or cm² instead of cm³.

example.question: Wanjiru builds a box shape using 24 cubes, each with edges of 1 cm. What is its volume?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..cause: The child treats the unit as a label to copy from the last topic, such as area, rather than as the kind of quantity being measured.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..reveals: Offer multiple choice with 24 cm, 24 cm² and 24 cm³. Also ask the child to match three measurements (a stick, a page, a box) to the three units.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..help: Show a 1 cm line, a 1 cm square and a 1 cm cube side by side. Have children say which one 'fills space' before writing any unit.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..error: The child thinks the small ³ means 3 cm, so a 1 cm³ cube has edges of 3 cm.

example.question: A cube has a volume of 1 cm³. How long is each of its edges?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..cause: The child reads the raised 3 as an ordinary number in the measurement instead of meaning 'cubic' (three dimensions).
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..reveals: Ask the child to draw or pick out a 1 cm³ cube from cubes of edge 1 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..help: Have children measure a real 1 cm cube with a ruler in all three directions and say 'one centimetre long, one wide, one high: one cubic centimetre'.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..error: The child thinks a heavier object must have a bigger volume.

example.question: A 1 cm cube of wood and a 1 cm cube of iron are placed on a table. Which one takes up more space?
example.correct_answer: They take up the same space: each is 1 cm³.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..cause: The child uses everyday 'bigger' to mean heavier or more, and does not yet separate volume (space) from mass.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..reveals: Ask about two objects of equal size but different materials, and include 'the heavier one' as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CM3_UNIT_IDENTIFY..help: Let children hold equal-sized cubes of different materials, such as wood, plasticine and stone, and check that each fits exactly into the same 1 cm space.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.error: In a picture of a cuboid, the child counts the squares on the visible faces instead of the cubes. Edge cubes get counted more than once and hidden cubes are missed.

example.question: A picture shows a cuboid made of 1 cm cubes. It is 3 cubes long, 2 cubes wide and 2 cubes high. What is its volume?
example.wrong_answer: 16 cm³ (6 + 6 + 4 squares on the front, top and side)

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.cause: The child sees the drawing as flat faces and does not picture the cubes as solid layers going back into the page.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.reveals: Use a picture-based question with the face-square total as a distractor, then ask the child to build the shape and recount.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.help: Build the pictured cuboid with real cubes, then take it apart layer by layer so children see each cube counted once.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.error: The child counts only the top or front layer of cubes and gives that as the volume.

example.question: A stack of 1 cm cubes has 3 layers, and each layer is 4 cubes long and 2 cubes wide. What is its volume?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.cause: The child counts only what they can see and does not realise that the layers below are also part of the shape.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.reveals: Give the single-layer count as a distractor. Ask 'How many layers are there?' before the total.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.help: Have children build one layer, count it, then add identical layers one at a time, saying the running total each time.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.error: The child thinks the same cubes take up more space when arranged taller or longer.

example.question: Otieno uses 12 cubes to make a cuboid 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 1 cm high. He rebuilds the same 12 cubes into one 3 cm long, 2 cm wide and 2 cm high. Which has the greater volume?
example.correct_answer: They are equal: both are 12 cm³.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.cause: The child judges by one striking dimension (height or length) instead of the total amount of space.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.reveals: Ask the child to compare two pictured arrangements of the same number of cubes, with 'the taller one' as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.VOLUME_COUNT_CM3_C.help: Have children rebuild one set of cubes into several shapes and count each time, recording that the total stays the same.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.error: The child adds the number of layers to the cubes in one layer instead of multiplying.

example.question: One layer of a cuboid has 4 rows of 3 cubes, which is 12 cubes. There are 5 such layers. How many cubes are there altogether?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.cause: The child does not yet see the layers as equal groups, so uses addition of the two numbers given.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.reveals: Use a table task: 'cubes in one layer' and 'number of layers' columns, then a 'total' column to fill in.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.help: Stack layers one by one and write 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. Then ask how to get 60 quickly, linking it to 12 × 5.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.error: The child believes a box standing on its end has a different volume from the same box lying flat.

example.question: A matchbox-shaped cuboid is 6 cm long, 2 cm wide and 1 cm high when lying flat. Achieng stands it on its end so it is 6 cm high. What is its volume now?
example.wrong_answer: It is bigger now because it is taller.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.cause: The child links 'height' with size and does not understand that the order of the three dimensions does not change the product.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.reveals: Ask the child to compare and explain using two pictures of the same cuboid in different positions.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_FORMULA_DER.help: Flip a real box, or use a digital model as the design suggests, and recalculate in each position to show the same product.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.error: The child adds the length, width and height instead of multiplying them.

example.question: Find the volume of a cuboid 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.cause: The child confuses volume with perimeter-style adding of lengths, or remembers 'use all three numbers' without the operation.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.reveals: Include the sum of the sides as a multiple-choice distractor. Ask the child to check by building it with cubes.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.help: Have the child build the 5 by 3 by 2 cuboid and count 30 cubes, then compare with their answer of 10.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.error: The child multiplies only the length and width, giving the area of the base as the volume.

example.question: Find the volume of a cuboid 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm high.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.cause: The child carries over the area rule (rows × columns) from Grade 4 and forgets the layers.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.reveals: Include the base area as a distractor, and ask 'How many layers did you use?'
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_CALC.help: Have children say each step aloud: 'cubes in one layer, times the number of layers'.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.error: The child multiplies a measurement in metres with others in centimetres without converting first.

example.question: A wooden box is 1 m long, 10 cm wide and 5 cm high. What is its volume in cm³?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.cause: The child uses the numbers and ignores the units, so does not notice that 1 m is 100 cm.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.reveals: Use a word problem with one dimension in metres, with the unconverted product as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.help: Have children circle every unit in the question and rewrite all lengths in cm before using the formula.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.error: The child multiplies every number in the word problem, including ones that are not lengths.

example.question: A box of chalk costs Sh 50. It is 10 cm long, 6 cm wide and 5 cm high. Find its volume.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.cause: The child grabs numbers without thinking about what each one means in the situation.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.reveals: Include irrelevant information, such as a price or a number of boxes not asked about, and the product including it as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBOID_VOLUME_PROB.help: Have children list 'length = , width = , height = ' from the story before calculating, crossing out numbers that are not lengths.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_FORMULA_DERIV.error: The child thinks a cube's volume in cm³ is the same number as its edge in cm. A related error is saying the volume cannot be found because only one measurement is given.

example.question: A cube has edges of 3 cm. What is its volume?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_FORMULA_DERIV.cause: The child does not see that a cube has length, width and height, which are all equal to the one edge given.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_FORMULA_DERIV.reveals: Ask a true-or-false question: 'A cube with 3 cm edges has a volume of 3 cm³.' Then ask the child to build it.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_FORMULA_DERIV.help: Have children build a 3 cm cube from 1 cm cubes and count 27. Then label its length, width and height, all 3 cm.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.error: The child multiplies the edge by 3 instead of multiplying the edge by itself three times.

example.question: A cube-shaped box has edges of 4 cm. Find its volume.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.cause: The child mixes up 'use s three times' with 's times 3', made worse by seeing the ³ in cm³.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.reveals: Include s × 3 as a multiple-choice distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.help: Have children write the full s × s × s with the number in every place, for example 4 × 4 × 4, before calculating.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.error: The child works out s × s, the area of one face, and gives that as the volume.

example.question: A cube-shaped box has edges of 4 cm. Find its volume.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.cause: The child carries over the area of a square from earlier work and forgets the layers.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.reveals: Include s × s as a distractor, and ask how many layers a 4 cm cube has.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.VOLUME.CUBE_VOLUME_CALC.M.help: Link it to layers: 4 × 4 = 16 cubes in one layer, and there are 4 layers, so 16 × 4 = 64.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.error: Compares the numbers and ignores the units, so thinks 500 ml is more than 2 l.

example.question: Which holds more: a 500 ml bottle of water or a 2 l bottle of cooking oil?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.cause: The child focuses on the size of the number and does not see the unit as part of the measurement.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.reveals: Pair a large number with a small unit against a small number with a large unit, and offer both as options.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.help: Put a real 500 ml bottle beside a 2 l bottle and pour one into the other, then always read the number and the unit together aloud.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.error: Treats any number on a package label as capacity, including grams.

example.question: Which label shows capacity: '500 g' on a sugar packet, '500 ml' on a milk packet, or '50 cm' on a ruler?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.cause: The child mixes up the unit symbols and links 'how much' with any label.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.reveals: Use an odd-one-out or sorting task with g, kg, ml, l and cm labels from real Kenyan packaging.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.help: Sort real packets and bottles into 'how heavy' (g, kg) and 'how much liquid it holds' (ml, l) piles.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.error: Chooses litres for tiny amounts, or ml for very large ones.

example.question: A nurse gives a child one spoon of cough syrup. Is the dose 5 ml or 5 l?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.cause: The child has no mental picture of how much 1 ml or 1 l actually is.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.reveals: Ask the child to choose the sensible unit for a familiar item, with one absurd option.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_IDENTIFY_UNIT.help: Show a 5 ml medicine spoon next to a 1 l packet of milk and let pupils pour both.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.error: Counts each small unlabelled mark on a scale as 1 ml.

example.question: A jug is labelled 200 ml and 300 ml, with three small marks in between. The water is at the third small mark above 200 ml. How much water is there?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.cause: The child carries over the habit of counting ones on a ruler and does not work out what each division is worth.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.reveals: Use a scale where divisions are worth 25 or 50 ml and include the 'counted ones' answer as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.help: Before reading, have pupils find the difference between two labelled marks, count the spaces and divide to find each mark's value.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.error: Reads the level while looking down at the jug, or with the jug tilted, and gets a reading that is too high or too low.

example.question: Juma looks down into a measuring jug from above and reads 300 ml. With his eyes level with the water on a flat table, the jug shows 250 ml. What is the correct reading?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.cause: The child does not know that a reading must be taken at eye level on a flat surface.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.reveals: In a practical task, the teacher watches how the child reads, then compares pupils' readings of the same jug.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_SCALE.help: Teach the routine 'jug flat on the table, crouch until your eyes are level with the water, then read'.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.error: Gives the number of fills as the capacity, instead of multiplying by the size of the measure.

example.question: Akinyi fills a cup using a 5 ml medicine spoon 8 times. What is the capacity of the cup?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.cause: The child counts the fills without linking each fill to its value in ml.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.reveals: Offer the number of fills as a distractor in multiple choice.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.help: Have pupils say a running total aloud as they pour: '5 ml, 10 ml, 15 ml ...'.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.error: Thinks the measuring container that needs more fills is the bigger one.

example.question: Cup A fills a jug in 4 cupfuls. Cup B fills the same jug in 6 cupfuls. Which cup holds more?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.cause: The child assumes 'bigger number means bigger' and does not grasp the inverse relationship between unit size and count.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.reveals: Use a compare-and-explain question where the larger count belongs to the smaller cup.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_MEASURE_BY_FI.help: Fill the same jug with a large cup and a small cup and ask why the small cup needed more pours.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_NO.error: Gives estimates that are wildly unrealistic.

example.question: Choose the best estimate for a cup of chai: 25 ml, 250 ml or 2 500 ml.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_NO.cause: The child has no remembered reference amounts (5 ml spoon, 250 ml cup, 500 ml bottle, 1 l packet).
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_NO.reveals: Offer options that differ by a factor of ten.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_NO.help: Display a class 'benchmark shelf' of a 5 ml spoon, 250 ml cup, 500 ml bottle and 1 l packet, and refer to it before every estimate.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_TA.error: Judges capacity by height alone, so thinks a tall thin container holds more than a short wide one.

example.question: A tall thin glass holds 200 ml and a short wide bowl holds 500 ml. Before measuring, which do you think holds more?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_TA.cause: The child attends to one dimension (height) and ignores width.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_TA.reveals: Use a compare task with a tall narrow container and a short wide one, then check by pouring.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.ML_ESTIMATE.M_TA.help: Pour the full glass into the bowl so pupils see the bowl is not yet full.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.L_ML_RELATIONSHI.cause: The child over-generalises from Grade 4 metres and centimetres (1 m = 100 cm).
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.L_ML_RELATIONSHI.reveals: Offer 100 as a distractor, or ask 'How many 100 ml cups fill a 1 l packet?' (answer: 10).
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.L_ML_RELATIONSHI.help: Pour ten 100 ml cupfuls into a 1 l container together and record 10 × 100 ml = 1 000 ml.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.L_ML_RELATIONSHI.error: Gives ½ l as 50 ml and ¼ l as 25 ml.

example.question: ½ l = ___ ml

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.L_ML_RELATIONSHI.cause: The child halves 100 instead of 1 000, linked to the 1 l = 100 ml idea.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.L_ML_RELATIONSHI.reveals: Ask the child to match ½ l and ¼ l containers to ml amounts, with 50 and 25 among the options.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.L_ML_RELATIONSHI.help: Use the Grade 4 ½ l and ¼ l containers and pour them into a ml-graduated jug to read 500 ml and 250 ml.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.CONVERT_L_TO_ML..error: Multiplies by 100 (adds two zeros) when changing litres to ml.

example.question: A jerrycan holds 4 l. How many ml is that?

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.CONVERT_L_TO_ML..cause: The child uses the m–cm multiplier from Grade 4.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.CONVERT_L_TO_ML..reveals: Offer the ×100 answer as a distractor.
MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.CONVERT_L_TO_ML..help: Have pupils write '1 l = 1 000 ml' at the top of every conversion and multiply by that fact.

MATH.G5.MEASUR.CAPACITY.CONVERT_L_TO_ML..error: Joins the digits together when converting a mixed amount, missing out the zero placeholder.

example.question: 2 l 50 ml = ___ ml
