MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.DEGREE_AS_UNIT.M_G.error: Judges angle size by the distance between the tips of the arms.

example.question: Angle A is 60° with arms 5 cm long; angle B is 80° with arms 1 cm long. Which is bigger?
example.wrong_answer: Angle A, because its arm ends are further apart

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.DEGREE_AS_UNIT.M_G.cause: Looks at the 'space' between the ends of the lines instead of the turn at the vertex.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.DEGREE_AS_UNIT.M_G.reveals: A pair where the smaller angle has the wider gap between arm ends.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.DEGREE_AS_UNIT.M_G.help: Model angles with a pair of strips joined at one end (or opened scissors) and ask how far one arm has turned, not how far apart the tips are.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.error: Reads the scale that does not start at 0 on the baseline arm, giving 180° minus the true angle.

example.question: One arm lies along the baseline through the 0 on the right. The other arm passes the marks labelled 60 and 120. What is the angle?

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.cause: Reads whichever number is outermost or most visible, without tracing from 0.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.reveals: Make 180° minus the true angle a distractor in every reading item, using acute angles that are clearly smaller than a right angle.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.help: Have the child put a finger on the 0 where the arm lies, follow that same scale round to the other arm, and then ask 'is it bigger or smaller than a right angle?'

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.error: Counts the small degree marks in the wrong direction from a labelled number.

example.question: Using the scale that starts at 0 on the baseline arm, the other arm is 3 small marks past 40, on the way to 50. What is the angle?

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.cause: On a two-direction scale the child counts down from 40, following the other scale's numbers or reading right to left by habit.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.reveals: Use readings that fall between labelled tens and include the 'counted back' value as a distractor.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.help: Ask the child to name the labelled numbers on either side of the arm first (40 and 50), so the answer must lie between them.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.error: Treats each small mark as more than 1°, for example as 10° or as 5°.

example.question: On the correct scale the arm is 2 small marks past 70, on the way to 80. What is the angle?

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.cause: Does not know that the space between two labelled numbers is split into 10 one-degree parts.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.reveals: Include readings just past a labelled ten, with a distractor that counts each mark as 10.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.READ_PROTRACTOR_BO.help: Get the child to count the small spaces between 0 and 10 on a protractor and conclude that each one is 1°.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.error: Lines the bottom edge of the protractor up with the arm instead of the 0° baseline, which on many protractors sits above the edge.

example.question: Measure angle ABC, which is 70°.
example.wrong_answer: A reading a few degrees out, e.g. 66°

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.cause: Treats the protractor like a ruler and uses its straight edge.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.reveals: A spot-the-error picture with the edge, not the baseline, on the arm; or practical results that are consistently a few degrees out.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.help: Have children trace the baseline on their own protractor with a finger before every measurement and check that the arm runs exactly along it.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.error: Places the protractor's centre point somewhere along an arm rather than exactly on the vertex.

example.question: Measure angle PQR, which is 50°.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.cause: Does not understand that the angle is the turn about the vertex, so the centre of the protractor must sit at that point.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.reveals: A spot-the-error image with the centre slid along one arm.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.help: Mark the vertex with a dot and insist the small centre mark or hole covers the dot before anything else is done.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.error: When neither arm is horizontal, keeps the protractor straight and reads only where the upper arm crosses the scale.

example.question: With the protractor held level, one arm crosses the scale at 20 and the other at 80 (same scale). What is the angle?

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.cause: Has learnt the procedure only for angles drawn with one arm horizontal, and does not see the angle as a gap between two readings.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.reveals: Tilted angles where the protractor cannot be put on 0 without turning it or the page.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.help: Show that the protractor (or page) may be rotated to put one arm on 0, and as a check, subtract the two readings.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.error: When the arms are too short to reach the scale, guesses the reading instead of extending the arms.

example.question: Measure the 35° angle drawn with arms only 1 cm long.
example.correct_answer: 35°, after extending the arms with a ruler

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.cause: Believes extending the arms would change the angle (linked to M_LONGER_ARMS_BIGGER).
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.reveals: Include short-armed angles in measuring tasks; a wide spread of answers shows guessing.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_WITH_PROTR.help: Demonstrate extending the arms lightly in pencil, measuring before and after to show the angle stays the same.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.error: Records an angle as a bare number or in centimetres.

example.question: Measure the angle between the ladder and the ground in the drawing.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.cause: Associates measuring with a ruler and length units.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.reveals: Open-response items that require the child to write the unit themselves.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.help: Have the child say 'degrees' aloud with every reading and write the ° symbol as part of the answer.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.error: Thinks that drawing a shape larger, or showing a bigger picture of a roof, makes its angles bigger.

example.question: A small drawing of a roof has a top angle of 100°. A larger drawing of the same roof is twice as big. What is its top angle?

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.cause: Applies the idea of scaling lengths to angles.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.reveals: Ask for angles in an enlarged copy of a shape; doubled values expose the error.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.help: Let children measure the same corner on a small and a large copy of a triangle and compare their results.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.error: Accepts a measurement that contradicts what the angle obviously looks like, for example recording an obtuse value for a sharp corner.

example.question: Measure the sharp corner of a triangular scarf drawing (true size 30°).

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.cause: Treats measuring as reading a number off a tool, with no prior estimate.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.reveals: Estimate-then-measure items; ask 'Is it more or less than a right angle?' before measuring.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.MEASURE_ANGLES_IN_.help: Make 'estimate first, using the corner of a book as a right angle' a fixed step in every measuring task.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.error: Recognises a right angle only when its arms are horizontal and vertical.

example.question: A square signboard at a Nairobi bus stop hangs tilted. Is the angle at its corner a right angle?
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is still a right angle (90°).

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.cause: Has mostly seen right angles drawn in the standard 'L' position.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.reveals: Pictures of right angles in rotated positions mixed with angles that are nearly, but not exactly, right angles.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.help: Have children test tilted corners with a folded paper right angle rather than judging by eye.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.error: Thinks the angle is the corner point itself rather than the amount of opening between two arms.

example.question: Show the angle made by an opened pair of scissors.
example.wrong_answer: Points only to the screw where the blades join.
example.correct_answer: Shows the opening between the two blades, which meet at the screw (the vertex).

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.cause: Confuses 'angle' with the everyday word 'corner' and with the vertex.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.reveals: Ask the child to mark an angle with an arc on a picture; marking a dot at the vertex reveals the error.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.help: Always mark angles with an arc between the arms and use the word 'vertex' for the meeting point.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.error: Does not see that a turning object, such as a door or a clock hand, makes an angle, because no lines are drawn.

example.question: A classroom door opens a quarter turn. What angle does it make with the closed position?

MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.cause: Associates angles only with drawn shapes and fixed corners, not with turning.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.reveals: Environment items about doors, gates, clock hands or a goat tethered and turning, rather than drawn figures.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.ANGLES.ANGLES_IN_ENVIRONM.help: Open the classroom door slowly and ask children to say when it has made a right angle, then show the two 'arms' (frame and door).

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.error: Calls any box-shaped object a cube, or cannot tell a cube from a cuboid.

example.question: Wanjiku has a building brick. Is it a cube or a cuboid?
example.correct_answer: A cuboid, because its faces are not all equal squares; some faces are long rectangles.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.cause: 'Cube' is learnt as a general word for 'box', without the condition that all faces are equal squares.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.reveals: Show a dice, a matchbox and a brick and ask which are cubes. A child with this idea picks all three.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.help: Have children press each face of a dice and a matchbox onto paper and compare: a cube's prints are all the same square.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.error: Recognises an object only in its usual position. For example, they do not recognise a cylinder lying on its side or a pyramid standing on its point.

example.question: A tin of Kimbo is lying on its side on the table. What 3-D object is it?
example.wrong_answer: It is not a cylinder now / a rectangle
example.correct_answer: It is still a cylinder; turning an object does not change its shape.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.cause: Pictures in books usually show cylinders upright and pyramids point-up, so the child links the name to one picture, not to the object's properties.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.reveals: Include pictures of familiar objects in unusual positions among the naming items and see whether accuracy drops.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.help: Let children turn real objects in their hands and name them in every position, and always include tilted or lying-down pictures in tasks.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.error: Thinks objects of very different size, colour or material cannot be the same shape.

example.question: Is a plastic water tank the same 3-D object as a tin of milk?
example.wrong_answer: No, the tank is much bigger.
example.correct_answer: Yes, both are cylinders: two flat circular ends and a curved surface.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.cause: The child classifies objects by everyday features such as size and use rather than by geometric shape.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.reveals: Ask the child to sort objects of mixed sizes (orange, football, marble, tin, tank picture). They group by size instead of by shape.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.help: Ask 'What stays the same if I make it bigger or smaller?' and sort big and small examples of each object together.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.error: Calls any object with a point at the top a pyramid, including cones such as an ice-cream cone or a round hut roof.

example.question: Is the roof of a round grass-thatched hut a pyramid?
example.correct_answer: No. A pyramid has flat triangular faces meeting at a point and a flat base with straight sides; the hut roof has a curved surface and a circular base.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.cause: The child focuses on one feature (the point) and ignores whether the surfaces are flat or curved.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.reveals: Odd-one-out task with a square-based pyramid, a triangular-based pyramid and a cone. The child cannot pick the cone.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.NAME_3D_OBJEC.help: Let the child run a finger over the sides: a pyramid has flat triangles and straight edges, but a cone has a curved surface.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.error: Describes a cylinder as having only curved surfaces (or only flat ones), missing that it has both.

example.question: Describe the surfaces of a tin of cooking fat.
example.wrong_answer: It is round, so all its surfaces are curved.
example.correct_answer: It has two flat circular surfaces (top and bottom) and one curved surface around the side.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.cause: The child describes the object by its overall 'roundness' instead of examining each surface separately.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.reveals: Ask whether a tin can stand without rolling and why. The child cannot connect standing on its end to a flat surface.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.help: Have the child stand a tin on its end, then roll it on its side, and say which surface touches the table each time.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.error: Counts only the top point of a pyramid as a corner and ignores the corners of the base.

example.question: How many corners does a square-based pyramid have?
example.correct_answer: 5 (one at the top and four around the square base)

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.cause: The apex is the most noticeable feature, and corners at the base are hidden or seen as part of the table.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.reveals: Ask for the number of corners on a pictured pyramid. A wrong answer of 1 exposes the error.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.help: Let children touch and mark each corner of a model pyramid with a small piece of plasticine or a sticker, including those at the bottom.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.error: Believes only a sphere can roll, or that an object either rolls or slides but cannot do both.

example.question: Which of these can roll: a football, a tin of milk, a matchbox?
example.correct_answer: The football and the tin. The tin rolls on its curved surface and can also slide or stand on its flat ends.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.cause: Rolling is linked with balls in everyday play, and the child does not link rolling to having a curved surface.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.reveals: Ask 'roll, slide, or both?' for each object. The child gives only one answer for the cylinder.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.DESCRIBE_3D_F.help: Do a simple ramp test with a book and real objects, then ask children to explain what kind of surface lets an object roll.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_PL.error: Uses the name of a flat shape for a solid object, such as 'circle' for a ball or 'square' for a dice.

example.question: What 3-D object is an orange?
example.correct_answer: A sphere. A circle is a flat shape; an orange is solid and round all over.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_PL.cause: Everyday language and early learning use 2-D names for objects, and the child has not separated flat shapes from solids.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_PL.reveals: Multiple-choice item with both 'circle' and 'sphere' (or 'square' and 'cube') as options.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_PL.help: Put a paper circle next to a ball and ask which one you can hold and turn, then insist on the correct name for each.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_TH.error: Thinks a thin real object, such as a coin, a chapati or a sheet of paper, is a 2-D shape.

example.question: Is a five-shilling coin a 2-D shape or a 3-D object?
example.correct_answer: 3-D. It is a very short cylinder with some thickness; its flat faces are circles.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_TH.cause: The child judges by how flat an object looks, not by whether it has thickness and takes up space.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_TH.reveals: Sorting task that includes thin objects. The child places a coin or paper with the drawn shapes.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_VS_3D.M_TH.help: Stack several coins to make a tall cylinder so the child sees each coin has thickness, then name the face (circle) and the object (cylinder) separately.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.error: When working from a picture, considers only the faces that can be seen and forgets the hidden ones.

example.question: Mwangi traces round every face of a cube-shaped box on paper. How many squares does he draw?

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.cause: The child treats the drawing as the whole object and cannot imagine the back, bottom and other hidden faces.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.reveals: Use a picture-only question that needs hidden faces. An answer of 3 for a cube shows the child is reading only the drawing.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.help: Pair every picture with a real box first, and let children tick off faces with chalk as they trace them.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.error: Says all the faces of a square-based pyramid are triangles and forgets the square base.

example.question: What 2-D shapes are the faces of a square-based pyramid?
example.correct_answer: Four triangles and one square (the base).

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.cause: The base rests on the table and is not seen as a face, and the triangles stand out.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.reveals: Ask the child to list all the flat shapes, or to choose which object made a square print.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.help: Lift the pyramid and press its base in paint or on sand to show the square print it leaves.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.error: Says a sphere has a circle as a face because its outline looks like a circle.

example.question: Which 2-D shape is a flat face of a football?
example.correct_answer: None. A sphere has one curved surface and no flat face (its outline only looks like a circle).

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.cause: The child confuses the outline seen in a picture with a flat face that could be traced or printed.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.reveals: Ask 'Which objects could leave a circle print in wet sand?' The child includes the ball.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.help: Try to trace round a ball and a tin on paper: only the tin's flat end gives a proper circle face.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.error: Says a cylinder has a rectangle face because its side view looks like a rectangle.

example.question: What flat shapes are found on a tin of Kimbo?
example.correct_answer: Two circles; the side is a curved surface, not a flat rectangle.

MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.cause: The child describes the outline of the side view rather than the actual surface, which is curved.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.reveals: A true/false item, 'A cylinder has a flat rectangular face'. Answering 'true' reveals the error.
MATH.G5.GEOMET.3_D_OBJECTS.2D_FACES_IN_3.help: Let the child lay a ruler against the curved side to see it does not lie flat, unlike the circular ends.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.error: Chooses categories where one includes another, so some items fit two categories.

example.question: Wanjiru will record vehicles passing the school gate using these categories: car, matatu, vehicle, motorcycle. What is wrong with her categories?
example.correct_answer: 'Vehicle' includes all the others, so a matatu could be recorded under 'matatu' or 'vehicle'. She should replace 'vehicle' with separate types such as lorry, bicycle or 'other'.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.cause: The child lists words linked to the topic without checking that each item belongs to exactly one category.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.reveals: Give a category list containing a general word and ask where a particular item (a matatu) should go; children with this error will not notice two possible places.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.help: Before collecting, ask learners to sort a few real examples into the categories and check that each one fits in exactly one place.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.error: Thinks only numbers count as data, so rejects information such as colours, foods or types of vehicle.

example.question: Which of these can be collected as data? A: the shoe sizes of 30 learners. B: the favourite foods of 30 learners. C: both A and B.
example.correct_answer: C. Favourite foods are data too: we count how many learners chose each food.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.cause: Mathematics is linked only with numbers, and counting the choices is not yet seen as producing data.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.reveals: Offer one numerical and one category data set in a 'which is data' item; option A exposes the error.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PLAN_.help: Collect a category set in class (for example favourite food: ugali, chapati, rice) and show that it becomes numbers once counted.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.error: Records some people or items twice, or misses some, and does not check the total against the number observed.

example.question: Juma asked his 30 classmates their favourite drink. He recorded: tea 12, uji 9, milk 8, juice 6. Is his record correct?
example.correct_answer: No. 12 + 9 + 8 + 6 = 35, but only 30 learners were asked, so some answers were recorded more than once.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.cause: The child does not see that the total of the records must equal the number of people or items observed.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.reveals: Give a record whose total does not match the stated number surveyed and ask whether it is correct.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.help: Have learners tick off each name on the class list as it is recorded, and add up the records at the end to compare with the class size.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.error: Writes each different value only once instead of recording every observation, so repeated values are lost.

example.question: Atieno asked 30 learners their shoe size and wrote down: 3, 4, 5, 6. What has gone wrong?
example.wrong_answer: Nothing is wrong. Those are the sizes.
example.correct_answer: She has recorded only the different sizes. She needs 30 entries, one for each learner (for example 4, 5, 4, 3, 5, ...), so that she can count how many learners wear each size.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.cause: The child sees the task as finding out which sizes exist rather than how many learners have each size.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.reveals: Ask how many learners wear size 4 using her record; the child with this error cannot answer, or says 1.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COLLE.help: Ask 'How many people did you ask? How many entries have you got?' so that learners see there must be one record per person.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.error: Draws a table without a title or column headings, so a reader cannot tell what the entries mean.

example.question: Achieng's table has two rows: 'Mango | 7' and 'Orange | 4'. A visitor asks, '7 what?' What should Achieng add?
example.correct_answer: A title such as 'Favourite fruits of Grade 5 learners', and the column headings 'Fruit' and 'Number of learners'.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.cause: The child knows what the numbers mean and does not think about a reader who did not collect the data.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.reveals: Show a table without headings and ask what is missing, or ask a learner to explain someone else's table.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.help: Swap tables between pairs and ask each pair to explain the other's table without talking to its owner; then add whatever was missing.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.error: Writes an entry in the row next to the one it belongs to, so values are paired with the wrong names or categories.

example.question: Record in a 'Name | Age' table: Otieno is 11, Akinyi is 10, Baraka is 12.
example.wrong_answer: Otieno | 10, Akinyi | 12, Baraka | (blank). The ages have slipped up one row.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.cause: The child fills the columns separately and does not read across each row, often because the rows are not ruled.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.reveals: After recording, ask 'How old is Akinyi?' and check whether the answer read from the table matches the data given.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.help: Insist on ruled rows, and have learners fill one complete row (name and age) before moving to the next.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.error: Draws five upright strokes and then a crossing stroke, so each 'gate' actually stands for six.

example.question: Show 7 using tally marks.
example.wrong_answer: [|||||/] || (five upright strokes plus a crossing stroke, then two more; this is 8)
example.correct_answer: [||||/] || (four upright strokes crossed by a fifth, then two strokes)

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.cause: The child remembers 'groups of five with a line across' but not that the crossing line is the fifth stroke.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.reveals: Ask the child to count every stroke in their gate aloud; a multiple-choice item can include the six-stroke gate as a distractor.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.help: Count aloud while drawing ('one, two, three, four, and FIVE goes across'), using bottle tops or sticks first.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.error: Draws a long row of single strokes without making groups of five, which makes counting slow and leads to mistakes.

example.question: Show 13 using tally marks.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.cause: The child sees tallies only as one mark for each item and not as a way to count quickly in fives.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.reveals: Show a long ungrouped row and a grouped tally and ask which is quicker to count, or time learners counting each.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.DRAW_.help: Let learners race to count 23 ungrouped strokes against 23 grouped ones, then discuss why the grouped tally was faster.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.error: Loses their place in the raw list, so some items are not tallied and others are tallied twice.

example.question: Tally these drinks: tea, uji, tea, milk, tea, uji, milk, tea, uji, tea.
example.wrong_answer: tea ||||, uji |||, milk || (only 9 marks; one tea was missed)
example.correct_answer: tea [||||/] (5), uji ||| (3), milk || (2). The total is 10, the same as the number of items in the list.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.cause: The child works through the list without marking which items have already been tallied.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.reveals: Ask whether the total number of tally marks equals the number of items in the list.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.help: Teach learners to cross out each item lightly as they tally it, and to check that the total number of marks equals the number of items.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.error: With numerical data, draws as many strokes as the value itself (for example 4 strokes for shoe size 4) instead of one stroke per learner.

example.question: Shoe sizes: 4, 5, 4, 6, 5, 4. Draw the tally for size 4.
example.wrong_answer: [||||/] [||||/] || (12 strokes: four for each of the three 4s)
example.correct_answer: ||| (3 strokes, because three learners wear size 4)

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.cause: The child mixes up the value being recorded (size 4) with how many times it occurs.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.reveals: Use numerical data in tallying tasks and ask how many learners the tally stands for.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.help: Have each learner say 'one stroke for me' as their size is tallied, so learners see that each mark stands for one person.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.error: Counts a gate as 4, counting only the upright strokes and ignoring the crossing stroke.

example.question: What number do these tallies show? [||||/] [||||/] ||

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.cause: The child sees the crossing line as a way of closing the group rather than as a stroke that counts.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.reveals: Include 10 (gates counted as 4) and 14 (gates counted as 6) as distractors.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.TALLY.help: Have learners count each gate aloud as 'five' and then count on in ones: 'five, ten, eleven, twelve'.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.error: Completes the frequency table without checking that the total frequency equals the number of items collected.

example.question: Data were collected from 30 learners. The frequencies in the table are 8, 11, 6 and 4. Is the table complete?
example.correct_answer: No. 8 + 11 + 6 + 4 = 29, so one learner is missing. The tallies should be checked again.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.cause: The child sees the total row as something to fill in, not as a check on the work.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.reveals: Give a table whose total is one less or one more than the stated number surveyed and ask whether it is correct.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.help: Make 'Does my total match the number I collected?' the final step every time a frequency table is prepared.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.error: Makes a new row for each observation, each with frequency 1, instead of one row per category.

example.question: Prepare a frequency table for these ages: 10, 11, 10, 10, 12, 11.
example.correct_answer: Three rows: Age 10 | 3, Age 11 | 2, Age 12 | 1. The total is 6.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.cause: The child copies the raw recording table from Grade 4 and does not see that the purpose of a frequency table is to group the same values together.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.reveals: Ask 'How many learners are 10?' and see whether the child has to add up rows to answer.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.PREPA.help: List the categories first (each value written once), then tally the data into them, and compare the result with the raw list.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.error: With numerical categories, gives the frequency when the question asks for the value, or gives the value when it asks for the frequency.

example.question: Age 10: 9 learners. Age 11: 14 learners. Age 12: 7 learners. Which age is the most common?

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.cause: Both columns contain numbers, and the child picks the largest number without checking what the column heading says.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.reveals: Ask 'which age' and 'how many learners' questions on the same table; the distractor is the number from the other column.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.help: Have learners point to the column heading and say what the question is asking for, an age or a number of learners, before they answer.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.error: Picks the category with the largest label, or the last row, as the most common instead of the one with the highest frequency.

example.question: Shoe size 3: 5 learners. Size 4: 12 learners. Size 5: 9 learners. Size 6: 4 learners. Which size is worn by the most learners?

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.cause: The child takes 'most' to mean the biggest number anywhere in the table, or the last row.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.reveals: Order the rows so that the largest label has the smallest frequency; children with this error choose the largest label.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.READ_.help: Ask learners to circle the largest number in the frequency column first, then read across to the category in that row.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.error: Adds the two frequencies when asked 'how many more'.

example.question: In 15 minutes, 12 matatus and 9 boda bodas passed the school. How many more matatus than boda bodas passed?

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.cause: The child hears the word 'more' and adds.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.reveals: Include the sum as a distractor in 'how many more' and 'how many fewer' items.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.help: Model the comparison by lining up 12 counters against 9 and asking how many are left without a partner.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.error: Gives the number of categories, or a single frequency, when asked how many were surveyed altogether.

example.question: Favourite drinks: tea 12, uji 8, milk 6, juice 4. How many learners were asked?

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.cause: The child counts the rows (the kinds of drink) rather than the learners.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.reveals: Offer the number of rows and the largest frequency as distractors.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.help: Ask 'What does each row stand for, and what does each number stand for?' before learners find the total.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.error: When asked how many did NOT choose a category, gives that category's own frequency.

example.question: Favourite drinks: tea 12, uji 8, milk 6, juice 4. How many learners did not choose tea?

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.cause: The child reads the category name in the question and does not notice the word 'not'.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.reveals: Use 'not' questions with the category's own frequency as a distractor.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.COMPA.help: Have learners underline 'not' and cover the tea row with a hand, then add up the rows that are left.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.error: Thinks that the most popular category must have been chosen by more than half of the group.

example.question: Favourite games of 30 learners: football 12, netball 8, volleyball 6, athletics 4. True or false: more than half of the learners chose football.
example.wrong_answer: True, because football is the most popular.
example.correct_answer: False. Half of 30 is 15, and 12 is less than 15. Football is the most chosen game, but most learners (18) chose something else.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.cause: The child treats 'most popular' and 'chosen by most learners' as the same thing.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.reveals: Ask a true-or-false item where the top category is below half the total.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.help: Have learners always find half of the total and compare the top frequency with it before saying 'most learners'.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.error: Applies a conclusion from one class to everyone, for example all children in Kenya.

example.question: In a survey of one Grade 5 class of 30, football was chosen by 12 learners, more than any other game. Which statement does the table support? A: All children in Kenya prefer football. B: In this class, more learners chose football than any other game.
example.correct_answer: B. The data are only about this class.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.cause: The child does not yet see that data describe only the group they were collected from.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.reveals: Include an overgeneralised statement among the options in a 'which statement is supported' item.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.help: Ask 'Who did we actually ask?' and have learners start their conclusions with 'In our class ...'.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.error: Makes a decision from personal preference instead of from the data in the table.

example.question: The canteen asked 30 learners for their favourite fruit: banana 11, mango 9, orange 6, pawpaw 4. Which fruit should the canteen buy most of?
example.wrong_answer: Mango, because it is the sweetest.
example.correct_answer: Banana, because the most learners (11) chose it.

MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.cause: The child does not yet see the purpose of collecting data, which is to base decisions on evidence rather than opinion.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.reveals: Ask for the answer and a reason; a reason that does not mention a number from the table shows the error.
MATH.G5.DATA_H.DATA_REPRESENTATION.INFER.help: Require every decision to be backed by a number from the table: 'I choose ___ because ___ learners chose it.'
